User of Meilisearch for ~6 months: delighted with performance and usability; uses a fraction of the resources of Elasticsearch; extensive, active language support; very active contributors on GitHub/Discord. Caveat: their cluster is small so can't comment on reliability at massive scale.
Cloud pricing complaint: generous free tier, but the next listed plan was $1200/month. (Pay-as-you-go beyond the free tier exists, but the free tier lacks high availability.)
Evaluating Meilisearch: without the replicated/distributed version available in the free tier, it is hard to really evaluate as a non-GC'd search engine.

Looked again at 1.0: the .NET client is still alpha, and it's very zero-configuration with no configurability of tokenization strategies. It replicates ~70% of their Elasticsearch setup with no config, which is impressive, but switching means giving up the other 30%.

Team tried Meilisearch for large datasets but couldn't plan RAM usage: low with few searches, but heavy search traffic could consume more than provisioned. Too unpredictable and expensive, so they went with Manticore instead.
Uses the core (Milli) in a local indexer for repositories and Obsidian files: works like a charm, indexing is surprisingly fast. The main thing missing is a typeahead feature.
In production for a few months and more than happy with reliability. Search speed and especially indexing speed increased a lot thanks to recent work.
Missing features blocking a switch from Elasticsearch: multi-index search (one search box across users/companies/tasks) and decay functions to phase out results by age or distance.

Used in production as the closest thing to self-hosted Algolia, but indexing constantly changing records was poor; it fell hours behind. With ~50k frequently changing ecommerce records it fell over, so they moved that part to Elastic. Rails gems also fell out of step with the server. Out-of-box search performance was better than Elastic and on par with Algolia.

Personal project (~200K tiny docs) integrated into WordPress via PHP: performance is great. Issues: default text matching too strict about word order; creating indexes, uploading and changing settings took about a week of coding; wanted search across multiple document types; default document and upload-size limits too low. Still made them very productive.

Has 15k documents, each ~70 pages of HTML text, currently on Elasticsearch/Searchkick. After 30 min with MeiliSearch: indexing ~10x faster, search at least 3x faster, literally zero config, uses 140MB RAM versus Elasticsearch needing 1–1.5GB+.

Criticism: hardly an Elasticsearch alternative since it doesn't scale beyond a single machine. Also objected to analytics being on by default (opt-out via MEILI_NO_ANALYTICS); argued it should be opt-in.

Early version supported only one filter: very fast but limited search, not great for anything remotely complex like searching with two conditions. Another user said the single-filter restriction had them leaning toward Manticore.
Algolia user asked whether MeiliSearch supports public API keys with encoded tenant filters. At the time it didn't, so all queries would need to go through their own servers to enforce filters.

Self-hosted on a Hetzner AX52 (64GB): ~80M documents across 13 indexes (~191GB), with main indexes of 5–10M records. Searches are fast and the server is 'bored'; it doesn't need RAM equal to index size. Early on, indexing couldn't keep up and CPU stayed pegged; Discord support helped and later batch indexing fixed it. Would recommend.

Uses Meilisearch in production with a 7 million article corpus and it works really well. Needed a 16GB machine for the initial import because batch indexing is memory intensive, then scaled down to half that RAM, and it remains very performant.
Tested recently: great experience; multi-index search in the frontend was very easy. Downside: no Australian cloud region, the closest is Singapore.
Used Coolify's one-click Meilisearch Docker install, sent 1,000,000 records, and it 'just worked' on an $8/mo Hetzner instance.

Happy production user for many years (notado.app), syncing Postgres records to Meilisearch. The older version is chugging along fine, but the new AI references don't inspire confidence. Picked it for the quality of multilingual search results.

Skeptic: HuggingFace's Meilisearch-backed quicksearch endpoint took 360ms to answer, questioning the 'instant search' claim. (A maintainer replied that most of the latency was waiting on OpenAI embeddings.)
